transcript:
Meeting header:
Date: 2026-09-06
Start: 14:30 PDT
Duration: ~58 minutes
Attendees: Priya (Redwood AE), Ethan (Redwood SE), Maya (Redwood CSM), Mark (CTO - HelioWorks), Dana (ML Eng), Sophie (Infra)
Link shared: https://redwood.app/pilot/helioworks/microburst-dashboard (shared screen during call)

Summary auto-gen (may be imperfect): focus on early token jitter, streaming handshake, and sequence-length driven kernel switches. Agreed on 10k run and kernel decision next week.

Transcript:
[00:00] Priya (Redwood AE): okay, hey everyone thanks for taking the time. Quick roll call, hi Mark, Dana, Sophie, are you all good?
[00:06] Mark (HelioWorks): Yep, here. Sorry running a minute behind but got it.
[00:09] Dana: here, ready.
[00:10] Sophie: hi all.
[00:12] Priya: great, cool. Agenda today is to review the latest TTFT microburst dashboard, walk through a couple kernel choices Ethan prepared, and lock down the pilot next steps. Anything to add?
[00:22] Mark: no, that's perfect. We really want to see if we can get median-first-byte down in the 50–60ms ballpark for our interactive agents without blowing up cost.
[00:31] Ethan (Redwood SE): yeah, and to add, we're especially looking at the streaming handshake overhead and the sequence length distribution you sent last week which had a long tail.
[00:40] Dana: that tail's from a subset of longer context support we keep for the dialogue history, yep.
[00:45] Priya: cool, okay Ethan you want to share the dashboard?
[00:47] Ethan: yes, sharing now. (screen) so this is the microburst view, top-left shows TTFT CDF by request class, you can see the green line is the canary kernel from last week, the orange is your prod profile.
[01:05] Sophie: quick question, what's the sampling frequency for these traces? Are we catching the entire KV cache warmups or just a 1% sample?
[01:13] Ethan: good call — these runs are from a 5% trace sample across the pilot fleet. We also have full trace exports for a 12-minute window that I can push.
[01:22] Priya: note, the KV cache is often transcribed as "K-V cash" in the logs so search terms might miss it, we had that in the last run, sorry, tmi.
[01:30] Mark: ha, noted.
[01:32] Dana: the orange line -- I'm seeing a shoulder at about 180ms, what is that likely corresponding to?
[01:38] Ethan: that aligns with requests that fall back to the fp16 kernel when sequence length goes above ~256 for that particular model. There's an extra memcpy and transform cost.
[01:46] Sophie: so the kernel flip is sequence-length triggered? I thought you had a hedging strategy.
[01:50] Ethan: yes we do hedge, but in the current pilot config hedging triggers at the queueing threshold; for this microburst bucket hedging didn't kick in before the kernel switch.
[02:01] Priya: and that causes the shoulder — model goes from fast matmul path to the other kernel which has a higher per-token latency.
[02:07] Mark: okay, that's a helpful root cause. Can hedging be tuned more aggressively?
[02:12] Ethan: we can, but there's a tradeoff: hedging earlier increases average cost. We estimate about +8–12% token cost if we hedge for sequences >=128 proactively.
[02:22] Dana: hmm, that cost hit is significant for our volume, but the user experience drop for 180ms spikes is also bad.
[02:29] Priya: understoood. That's why we'll ask you to run the 10k sample with explicit seqlen bins, so we can quantify tail probs and cost delta.
[02:38] Mark: yes please. Also can you annotate the traces with region/az and instance type? We suspect a networking oscillation on one AZ.
[02:46] Ethan: absolutely, the export includes AZ and instance id. I'll make sure the CSV includes those fields.
[02:52] Maya (Redwood CSM): quick note, we'll also attach the config used for the run so you can reproduce the analysis.
[02:57] Mark: perfect.
[03:00] [03:00] Speaker 1: (inaudible)
[03:03] Ethan: okay next up, kernel tradeoffs. I prepared two short slides — one is aggressive quantized kernel (INT8-ish path) and one is fp16 fused matmul.
[03:13] Ethan: the quantized path reduces median per-token by about 18% in isolated benchs but can increase variance on the first token because quant paths sometimes need extra dequant/reshape work when KV is cold.
[03:25] Dana: do you have numbers for T-T-F-T on that path specifically?
[03:29] Ethan: yes, sample bench shows TTFT median 42ms quant vs 52ms fp16, but 95th is 210ms quant vs 160ms fp16 in some microburst conditions. So quant helps median but hurts tail in noisy networking scenarios.
[03:45] Priya: and the reason is the extra transform on the first attention call when the kernel selection changes under load.
[03:51] Sophie: interesting. Could we combine — e.g., use fp16 for the first N tokens then switch to quant for bulk?
[03:57] Ethan: we can, that's a staged path. It requires session-aware kernel orchestration and introduces complexity for batching, but it's feasible. We'll need to simulate with your workload to see real gains.
[04:09] Mark: that staged approach might be our preferred tradeoff, accept slightly higher per-token cost for consistent first-token latency then save on bulk cost.
[04:16] Dana: yes we have long generations sometimes, so bulk token cost matters.
[04:20] Priya: okay noted. We'll include a simulation of staged path in the kernel tradeoff doc.
[04:24] [04:24] Speaker 2: (overlap)
[04:26] Ethan: moving on to streaming handshake — the other contributor to TTFTs is the early bytes buffering and the transport handshake. In the pilot we saw 30–40ms extra in some paths due to small MTU fragmentation and application-side reassembly delays.
[04:42] Sophie: on our infra side we do MSS clamping for some bursting streams; could that be adding latency?
[04:47] Ethan: yes that can add small delays especially when combined with Nagle or delayed ACKs. The dashboard shows some flows with 3–4ms extra per packet, which compounds.
[04:56] Mark: any low-hanging network config we can try?
[04:59] Ethan: disable Nagle for those clients, ensure TCP_NODELAY on the client sockets, and for the servers make sure delayed ACK timer is tuned. Also increase streaming buffer prefetch so first chunk arrives assembled.
[05:12] Sophie: we can try socket opts quickly, not a big lift. Could you send a recommended config snippet?
[05:17] Ethan: yes I'll paste it in the notes. (chat) sending now.
[05:20] Dana: switching topic — sequence-length distribution you saw had 12% above 512. Can we reduce history window without hurting accuracy?
[05:29] Mark: product-wise we can trim some of the explicit long-history, but we want an automated policy, maybe only keep last 3 turns if tokens exceed threshold.
[05:38] Priya: Redwood Optimize can run synthetic prompt sampling to estimate accuracy impact for history trimming; we can include that as a small eval.
[05:46] Dana: good. If we can keep the >512 bucket under 4% that would probably avoid many kernel flips.
[05:53] Ethan: agree. We'll also run a quick sensitivity analysis in the 10k sample to show the tail drop.
[05:58] [06:00] Speaker 3: (crosstalk)
[06:02] Sophie: another infra note — we saw one instance had higher CPU steal during the run. Could that be related?
[06:08] Ethan: yes, CPU steal/host contention will bump TTFT. We'll mark those instances in the trace so you can correlate.
[06:15] Priya: for the 10k run please include host-level metrics: CPU steal, NIC drops, and process-level GC if any.
[06:23] Mark: will do.
[06:25] Ethan: quick question for you Mark — what success criteria do we want to sign off this pilot on? Are we aiming for 75ms P50 TTFT or a 95% under 200ms?
[06:36] Mark: product says P50 under 80ms is our bar, but infra wants 95th under 200ms. If we can show both with reasonable cost, we greenlight production.
[06:45] Priya: ok that's helpful. We'll target both metrics in the tradeoff deck.
[06:50] Dana: on cost transparency, can Redwood surface expected per-million token uplift if we enable earlier hedging?
[06:56] Ethan: yes that's in the optimize workbook; I'll include a delta column for hedging policies. Expect around +8–12% for early hedge at seqlen 128 as mentioned.
[07:06] Priya: and one more operational ask — can we get audit logs of kernel flips per request id so your team can pinpoint user queries that tripped the switch?
[07:15] Ethan: yes, we can attach a kernel_switch boolean to the request trace and include the exact sequence length. That will be in the export.
[07:22] Sophie: excellent.
[07:25] [07:25] Speaker 1: (inaudible)
[07:27] Mark: any blockers for the 10k run?
[07:30] Dana: only that we need the config that Redwood used so we can mirror it; Maya said you'll attach that?
[07:35] Maya: yes will attach run config and the SDK call patterns we used.
[07:39] Priya: perfect. Next up — timeline and kernel decision. We propose a short kernel decision meeting next Tue 9/13, 11am PT to pick either staged fp16->quant or keep fp16 and focus on stream tuning. That meeting should include Sophie and one infra engineer, Dana and Mark from product.
[07:58] Mark: tentative yes, that time works for us.
[08:00] Dana: okay slot it.
[08:02] Ethan: I'll prepare a one-page pros/cons with cost delta and TTFT numbers for both options.
[08:08] Priya: great. Anything else?
[08:11] Sophie: can we get the initial microburst trace export by EOD tomorrow? If we can look overnight that's helpful.
[08:18] Ethan: yes I'll push the raw traces and CSV by EOD.
[08:22] Mark: thanks.
[08:24] Priya: recap real quick: Redwood shares dashboard + traces by EOD tomorrow, HelioWorks runs 10k sample with seqlen bins and host metrics by Fri 9/10, Redwood shares kernel tradeoff doc by Thu 9/9, and we'll have kernel decision meeting Tue 9/13. Anything I missed?
[08:40] Dana: sounds right.
[08:42] Sophie: yep.
[08:44] Mark: good.
[08:45] Priya: awesome. We'll close there, thanks everyone.
[08:49] Maya: thanks all.
[08:51] [08:51] End of recording

Notes on transcription: occasional mis-hearings of acronyms (e.g., T-T-F-T vs TTFT) and product names may be inconsistent. Speaker labels are best-effort.
